issues: Significance overstates: 'turned data protection from a Hessian and Swedish experiment into a European norm with a licensing regulator in each country'. West Germany already had a federal act (BDSG, 1977; Paperjam lists Germany in 1977), and the 1978-79 laws did not all license: West Germany's federal commissioner, Austria's register and commission, and France's CNIL were not uniform licensing systems. Norway itself did use licensing (konsesjon), per the Føyen article.

Date nuance: Norwegian statutes carry the date of royal sanction in the Council of State, and 9 June 1978 was a Friday (the Council's regular day), so the Lagting's vote may have come a few days earlier. The Lov & Data source does literally say 'vedtatt av Stortinget den 9. juni 1978', so the quote stands, but the summary is reworded so it is true either way. Lovdata's statute page (HTTP 405) could not be read to settle this.

fieldFixes.summary: Norway's Personal Data Registers Act (personregisterloven) is dated 9 June 1978; it followed two government inquiries, NOU 1974: 22 on personal data and privacy and NOU 1975: 10 on public personal-data systems. Before it could take effect, regulations had to be drafted and a Data Inspectorate (Datatilsynet) set up. A working group did both so that the law could enter into force with its regulations on 1 January 1980. Businesses then needed a licence (konsesjon) from Datatilsynet to set up new personal registers. In the same year, 1978, Denmark, France and Austria also legislated.
fieldFixes.significance: Part of the 1978-79 wave that spread data protection from Hesse, Sweden and West Germany's 1977 federal act across Western Europe, usually with a dedicated supervisory authority. Norway, like Sweden, chose a licensing model.

fieldFixes.summary: The Council of Europe's Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data (ETS No. 108) was opened for signature in Strasbourg on 28 January 1981. Its purpose is to secure for every individual, whatever their nationality or residence, respect for their rights and freedoms, in particular their right to privacy, with regard to automatic processing of personal data, which it calls 'data protection'. Seven states signed it first, and it entered into force in 1985. Since 2007 the anniversary, 28 January, has been marked each year as European Data Protection Day.
fieldFixes.significance: Data protection became a binding treaty obligation, open to non-European states by invitation, and 28 January is still marked as Data Protection Day.

issues: Imprecise: 'It voided the census act's provisions for passing data to population registers'. The operative part voids § 9(1) to (3), which covered transfers of census data to other authorities. § 9(1) allowed comparison with municipal civil registers, and (2) and (3) allowed further transfers; headnote 3 reads 'The legal provisions governing the transfer of data under § 9(1) to (3) ... (including the comparison of census data with civil registry records)'. The court also upheld the survey programme itself (§ 2 nos. 1-7, §§ 3-5), which the summary leaves out. Reworded.

Everything else is confirmed: 15 December 1983, First Senate, the file numbers, the headnote language, the 27 April 1983 census date, the injunction, the 'Meine Daten gehören mir' slogan and the 1987 census (bpb: May 1987).

fieldFixes.summary: Citizens' initiatives and public figures had called for a boycott of the West German census set for 27 April 1983, with slogans such as 'Meine Daten gehören mir' ('My data belongs to me'). The Federal Constitutional Court suspended the count by injunction. In its judgment of 15 December 1983 (1 BvR 209/83 and others), the First Senate held that in the context of modern data processing, the general right of personality protects the individual against the unlimited collection, storage, use and sharing of personal data. It gives each person the authority, in principle, to decide on the disclosure and use of their data. The court upheld the survey itself. It voided § 9(1)-(3) of the census act, which let census data be passed to other authorities, including for comparison with population registers, and it required additional procedural safeguards. The census was finally held in 1987.
